aliases: Kepler's ellipse law and area law

milestones.label: Mysterium cosmographicum: polyhedra model of the orbits
milestones.description: Kepler's first cosmology tried to explain planetary distances by nested regular solids, the circle-based scheme his later laws replaced.

evidence.claim: Describes the Tubingen 1596 Mysterium cosmographicum and its nested-solids model.

milestones.note: Only a precursor: it is not the ellipse geometry.

milestones.label: Astronomia nova: elliptical Mars orbit and equal-area law
milestones.description: The book published the ellipse with the Sun at a focus and the equal-areas-in-equal-times rule, derived from Mars observations; these became the first and second laws.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1609 Astronomia nova edition.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Astronomia nova aitiologetos, 1609

evidence.claim: Open Library lists a 1609 Astronomia nova.
evidence.source: Open Library search: Astronomia nova entries

evidence.claim: States that Mars' orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at a focus and that the area law is in the 1609 book.

milestones.note: This single book is also the first purposeful application of conic geometry to planetary orbits, so no separate first_application is recorded. The 1609 book treats Mars; extension to all planets came later (Epitome, not checked).

milestones.label: Harmonices mundi: third law (period squared ~ radius cubed)
milestones.work: Kepler, Harmonices mundi libri V, Linz, 1619
milestones.description: Book V of the Harmony of the World states the relation between the squares of periods and the cubes of mean orbital radii.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1619 Harmonices mundi.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Harmonices mundi libri V, 1619

evidence.claim: Open Library lists a 1619 Harmonices mundi.
evidence.source: Open Library search: Harmonices mundi entries

evidence.claim: The Harmony of the World contains the third law, discovered while it was in press.

milestones.label: Principia: orbits from an inverse-square force
milestones.description: Newton derived Kepler's laws from universal gravitation, turning the empirical laws into consequences of dynamics and starting celestial mechanics proper.

evidence.claim: Open Library lists the 1687 Principia.
Discusses the inverse-square force and conic orbits in Book 1 of the Principia, 1687.

notes: English Wikipedia pages for the laws were not retrievable (API rate limit), so the stages come from the MacTutor Kepler and Newton biographies. The name 'Kepler's laws' (naming) and any institution milestone were not located; none recorded. The harvest summary says 'conic geometry into astronomy' which is consistent with the 1609 book but the Apollonian conic background (Kepler's Ad Vitellionem paralipomena 1604) was not checked. Epitome astronomiae Copernicanae (extension to all planets) not verified.

canonicalName: Kepler's Nova stereometria doliorum vinariorum (infinitesimal volumes of solids of revolution)

milestones.label: Nova stereometria doliorum vinariorum published
milestones.work: Kepler, Nova stereometria doliorum vinariorum, Linz, 1615
milestones.description: Kepler computed volumes of many revolved solids by treating them as sums of infinitely many thin pieces, following Archimedes and motivated by gauging wine barrels.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1615 Linz edition.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Nova stereometria doliorum vinariorum, 1615

evidence.claim: Says the Linz 1615 study of solids of revolution used a resolution into indivisibles and is part of the ancestry of infinitesimal calculus.

milestones.note: Written after his 1613 wedding wine purchase (MacTutor), published 1615.

milestones.label: Cavalieri's Geometria indivisibilibus builds on Kepler
milestones.work: Cavalieri, Geometria indivisibilibus continuorum nova quadam ratione promota, Bologna, 1635
milestones.description: Cavalieri's theory of indivisibles developed Archimedes' exhaustion with Kepler's infinitely small quantities, systematising what Kepler did case by case.

evidence.claim: The 1635 theory incorporates Kepler's infinitesimally small geometric quantities.
Says Kepler's barrel method was later developed by Cavalieri.

milestones.note: Year from MacTutor; Open Library only shows a 1653 edition.

works.whyItMatters: Volumes by summation of infinitesimal pieces

notes: Wikipedia page for the book returned an empty extract and other Wikipedia pages were rate-limited. Archimedes' Method is the classical precursor (not dated here). Crossref lists a 2019 translation review (Isis 10.1086/702466) confirming the title but not the 1615 date. Only two milestones are supported; no naming or institution found. The harvest label 'calculus (precursor)' is a catalogue label, not a milestone.

milestones.label: Mirifici logarithmorum canonis descriptio
milestones.work: Napier, Mirifici logarithmorum canonis descriptio, Edinburgh, 1614
milestones.description: Napier published the idea of logarithms with a table of logarithms of sines, reducing multiplication and division to addition and subtraction.

evidence.claim: Crossref lists the 1614 Descriptio (digitised copy).
evidence.source: Crossref record: Smithsonian Libraries record, issued 1614

evidence.claim: Open Library lists the 1614 Descriptio.
States that Napier first published the concept with tables in the 1614 Descriptio, though Burgi approached it.
evidence.source: English Wikipedia: Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio

evidence.claim: Napier's discussion appears in the 1614 Descriptio.

milestones.note: Joost Burgi arrived independently at a related idea; his Progress Tabulen appeared in 1620 (not verified here).

milestones.label: Napier and Briggs agree on base-ten logarithms
milestones.description: Briggs, struck by the Descriptio, proposed a scale with log 1 = 0 and log 10 = 1 and discussed the change with Napier.

evidence.claim: Quotes Briggs' 1615 letter and says the change to log 1 = 0 came from Napier-Briggs discussions.
Briggs proposed base-10 logarithms at Gresham College after reading the Descriptio.

milestones.note: Year is of the letter; exact timing of the decimal proposal is not fixed.

milestones.label: Mirifici logarithmorum canonis constructio published
milestones.description: The companion volume explains how the tables were built from geometric progressions, and uses a decimal point.

evidence.claim: Constructio published by Napier's son in 1619.
evidence.source: English Wikipedia: Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio

evidence.claim: Open Library lists a Constructio dated 1620 (probably an edition date).

milestones.note: Open Library shows 1620; Wikipedia says 1619; kept 1619 with this conflict flagged.

milestones.label: Briggs' Arithmetica logarithmica
milestones.description: The first large published table of common logarithms (to 14 places for 1-20,000 and 90,000-100,000), which made logarithms standard working tools.

evidence.claim: Record of Arithmetica logarithmica 1624.
Describes the 1624 work and its table ranges.

notes: No dated naming milestone found: the coinage of the word 'logarithm' by Napier was not verified (Wikipedia Logarithm page rate-limited). The catalogue type 'birth-by-fusion' (progressions, geometry, trigonometry) is not directly sourced. Wright's English translation of the Descriptio (1616) exists per MacTutor but is not a separate milestone.

canonicalName: Fermat's adequality (method of maxima, minima and tangents)
aliases: Methodus ad disquirendam maximam et minimam
Fermat's method of maxima and minima

milestones.label: Early maxima and minima work in Bordeaux
milestones.description: In Bordeaux Fermat produced maxima-and-minima work, passed to a local mathematician, before the Methodus circulated.

evidence.claim: Places his first work on maxima and minima in Bordeaux, with Plane loci given c. 1629.

milestones.note: MacTutor does not give an exact year for the maxima work; 1629 is the date of the neighbouring Plane loci gift.

milestones.label: Methodus circulated in manuscript
milestones.work: Fermat, Methodus ad disquirendam maximam et minimam (circulated c. 1636)
milestones.description: Fermat equated p(x) and p(x+e) approximately, divided by e and dropped remaining e-terms to find extrema and tangents; the text circulated privately.

evidence.claim: States the treatise circulated in France c. 1636 and describes the method.

milestones.note: Private circulation, hence a precursor. Fermat also argued with Descartes about it in 1637-38 (MacTutor).

milestones.label: Hérigone prints Fermat's maxima and minima method
milestones.description: Hérigone's course added a supplement carrying Fermat's method, its first public appearance.

evidence.claim: Says Hérigone added a supplement with Fermat's methods of maxima and minima to his Cursus mathematicus.

milestones.note: Year 1642 is from background knowledge, not from the pages read; Internet Archive shows Cursus editions dated 1639 and 1644. Treat as open until the supplement's imprint year is checked.

milestones.label: Varia opera mathematica prints Methodus
milestones.description: The posthumous collected works first gave the Methodus and related tracts in print in full.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1679 Varia opera mathematica.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Varia opera mathematica, 1679

evidence.claim: Open Library lists Varia opera 1679.
evidence.source: Open Library search: Varia opera entries

milestones.note: That the Methodus itself is in the 1679 volume rests on the MacTutor reference to the 1679 Maxima et minima extract; contents not checked page by page.

people.name: Rene Descartes
people.roleNote: Critic and rival method of normals

notes: Scholars disagree about what adequality means (Wikipedia notes this). The adequality name is Fermat's own, borrowed from Diophantus (Wikipedia). Whether 1642 or 1679 is the first print is open; no naming milestone beyond Fermat's own term. The 'differential calculus (precursor)' label stays a label, not a milestone.

milestones.label: Barrow's Lectiones geometricae
milestones.description: Barrow's lectures, edited by Collins, give a tangent method close to calculus and recognise integration and differentiation as inverse.

evidence.claim: Lectiones Geometricae published 1670; Barrow first to recognise differentiation and integration as inverse operations.

milestones.note: MacTutor claims Barrow as first to recognise the inverse relation; recorded as a precursor, not verified independently.

milestones.label: Newton's De methodis serierum et fluxionum written
milestones.work: Newton, De methodis serierum et fluxionum (written 1671; printed 1736)
milestones.description: Newton unified area, tangent, length and extremum problems under the method of fluxions, with integration as the inverse of differentiation, but kept it unpublished.

evidence.claim: Method of fluxions; De methodis written 1671, not printed until Colson's 1736 translation.

milestones.note: Newton's foundations date earlier (1660s, MacTutor); private, so a precursor and not a derived date.

milestones.label: Leibniz, Nova methodus pro maximis et minimis
milestones.work: Leibniz, Nova methodus pro maximis et minimis, itemque tangentibus, Acta Eruditorum, 1684
milestones.description: The first published account of the differential calculus, with the d notation and rules for powers, products and quotients (no proofs).

evidence.claim: Leibniz published the differential calculus in Acta Eruditorum in 1684.
Article on dating and numbering the editions of the Nova methodus (October 1684).
evidence.source: Crossref record: Printing Leibniz's Calculus, The Library 2021

milestones.note: The Crossref entry is a scholarly article about the 1684 printing, not the original.

milestones.label: Leibniz's integral calculus with the integral sign in print
milestones.description: A 1686 paper gave the integral calculus and the first printed use of the integral sign.

evidence.claim: 1686 Acta paper with first printed integral sign.

milestones.label: L'Hôpital, Analyse des infiniment petits
milestones.work: L'Hôpital, Analyse des infiniment petits, Paris, 1696
milestones.description: The first textbook of the differential calculus, based on Johann Bernoulli's lessons.

evidence.claim: Record shows the 1716 edition of the Analyse (first edition year not shown).
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Analyse des infiniment petits, 1716 edition

milestones.note: The 1696 first-edition year is background knowledge; only a 1716 edition was found. Needs a first-edition record.

milestones.label: Newton's fluxion tract first printed
milestones.work: Newton, Analysis per quantitatum series, fluxiones, 1711
milestones.description: Newton's early analysis appeared in print only in 1711, after the priority dispute had begun.

evidence.claim: MacTutor shows the title page of Analysis per quantitatum series fluxiones (1711).

milestones.note: Contents/composition date of the 1711 printing not checked beyond the title-page caption.

notes: Newton-Leibniz priority is disputed; by the schema private Newton work is a precursor, so conceptual date is Leibniz 1684. Wikipedia Calculus intro (saved lead) used only as a definition. Fermat's adequality and Cavalieri/Wallis indivisibles are separate events and not repeated. Naming of 'calculus' not dated; no institution milestone recorded.

milestones.label: Kepler's barrel stereometry
milestones.description: Kepler's infinitesimal summations were a model Cavalieri drew on.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1615 edition.
Cavalieri's theory incorporates Kepler's infinitesimals.

milestones.label: Cavalieri's Geometria indivisibilibus
milestones.work: Cavalieri, Geometria indivisibilibus continuorum nova quadam ratione promota, Bologna, 1635
milestones.description: Cavalieri presented areas and volumes as sums of indivisible chords or sections, giving quick rules for many figures.

evidence.claim: Presented in 1635 (manuscript finished December 1627).
Torricelli biography confirms 1635 publication.

milestones.note: Open Library shows only a 1653 edition; the 1635 year rests on MacTutor.

milestones.label: Torricelli's Opera geometrica
milestones.description: Torricelli adopted the method, proved it with extra rigour and applied it to new solids.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1644 Opera geometrica.
Torricelli studied Cavalieri's method, was first suspicious, then used it.

milestones.note: Specific new results of Torricelli (e.g. infinite solid) not checked here.

milestones.label: Cavalieri's Exercitationes geometricae sex
milestones.description: Cavalieri's improved exposition answering critics became the 17th-century source text.

evidence.claim: Exercitationes geometricae sex (1647) became the main source for 17th-century mathematicians.

milestones.label: Wallis's Arithmetica infinitorum
milestones.description: Wallis replaced geometric indivisibles by arithmetic summation, giving the product for pi/2 and integrals of powers.

evidence.claim: Arithmetica infinitorum 1656 with the pi product; Wallis studied Cavalieri, Roberval and Torricelli.

milestones.note: Internet Archive search found no 1656 record.

milestones.label: Roberval's Traité des indivisibles printed
milestones.work: Roberval, Traité des indivisibles, in Divers ouvrages, 1693
milestones.description: Roberval's independent treatise (he claimed an Archimedean basis) computed integrals of powers and sine; printed long after composition.

evidence.claim: Published in the 1693 Divers ouvrages; Roberval claimed it did not depend on Cavalieri.

milestones.note: Priority between Roberval and Cavalieri is a dispute; this is publication year only.

notes: Wikipedia Cavalieri pages rate-limited; stages from MacTutor biographies. No naming or institution milestone found. Guldin's critique of Cavalieri (MacTutor) is context, not a milestone. Pascal's 1658 cycloid work with indivisibles (MacTutor) could be added as an application; not verified in detail.
searchedSources: MacTutor Cavalieri, Torricelli, Wallis, Roberval, Pascal

milestones.label: Fermat's restoration of Apollonius' Plane loci
milestones.work: Fermat, Ad locos planos et solidos isagoge (circulated in manuscript)
milestones.description: Fermat translated loci problems into equations in the 1620s-30s; the Isagoge circulated only in manuscript and was printed after his death.

evidence.claim: Gave a copy of his Plane loci restoration in Bordeaux in 1629; the Isagoge appears among his works.

milestones.note: Year is the Plane loci gift; the Isagoge's own date was not read. Private, so precursor.

milestones.label: Descartes, La Geometrie
milestones.work: Descartes, La Geometrie, appendix to Discours de la methode, Leiden, 1637
milestones.description: Descartes applied algebra to geometry, solving construction problems through equations and classifying curves by degree.

evidence.claim: La Geometrie published at Leiden in 1637 and gave Cartesian geometry.
Record of the 1637 Discours de la methode volume.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Discours de la methode, 1637

milestones.note: Fermat's circulated manuscript has priority arguments; public print favours Descartes.

milestones.label: Van Schooten's Latin edition of the Geometria
milestones.work: van Schooten, Geometria a Renato Des Cartes (Latin ed.), 1649/1659
milestones.description: Van Schooten's annotated Latin version spread Descartes' method across Europe.

evidence.claim: Records show the Latin Geometria with commentary (1659 and 1683 editions found).
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Geometria a Renato Des Cartes, 1659 edition

milestones.note: The first (1649) edition year is background knowledge; only 1659 and 1683 records found.

milestones.label: Fermat's Isagoge printed in Varia opera
milestones.description: Fermat's analytic geometry reached print in the posthumous collected works.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1679 Varia opera mathematica.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Varia opera mathematica, 1679

evidence.claim: MacTutor lists the first page of Ad locos planos et solidos isagoge among Fermat's materials.

milestones.note: That the Isagoge sits in the 1679 volume is background knowledge, not checked in the scan.

milestones.label: Euler, Introductio in analysin infinitorum
milestones.description: Euler's textbook systematically treats curves through equations and functions, fixing modern analytic geometry.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1748 Introductio.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Introductio in analysin infinitorum, 1748

milestones.note: Whether it is the first systematic treatment is not established; recorded as a later consolidation.

works.citation: Ad locos planos et solidos isagoge, printed 1679
Geometria a Renato Des Cartes, Latin edition

notes: Wikipedia Analytic geometry and La Geometrie pages were rate-limited; the stages come from MacTutor. The term 'analytic geometry' was not dated (naming open). The Isagoge date, Fermat priority and van Schooten's first edition year remain open. Note that van Schooten's biography slug is not in MacTutor reads; his person link points to Descartes' page.

canonicalName: Fermat's number theory (little theorem, sums of squares, Fermat correspondence)

milestones.label: Bachet's Diophantus edition
milestones.work: Bachet, Diophanti Alexandrini Arithmeticorum libri sex, 1621
milestones.description: Fermat annotated a copy of this edition, the source of his observations.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1621 Bachet edition.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Diophanti Arithmeticorum libri sex, 1621

evidence.claim: Fermat's marginal notes relate to Bachet's edition of Diophantus.

milestones.label: Fermat's letters to Frenicle: little theorem
milestones.description: Fermat stated the theorem in private letters to Frenicle.

evidence.claim: Article reconstructing the Frenicle-Fermat correspondence of 1640.
Lists the Frenicle-Fermat 1640 correspondence in its references.

milestones.note: Private letters = precursor. The exact content (little theorem) comes from the standard account, with only the article title read here.

milestones.label: Samuel Fermat publishes Diophantus with Fermat's notes
milestones.work: Bachet-Fermat, Diophanti Alexandrini Arithmeticorum libri sex ... cum observationibus P. de Fermat, Toulouse, 1670
milestones.description: Fermat's marginal observations, including the Last Theorem statement, became public through his son's 1670 edition.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1670 edition with Fermat's observations.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Diophanti Arithmeticorum libri sex, 1670

evidence.claim: Marginal notes became known when Samuel published them in 1670.

milestones.note: Whether the little theorem itself is printed there is not checked.

milestones.label: Varia opera mathematica
milestones.description: First collected edition of Fermat's mathematical writings.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1679 Varia opera.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Varia opera mathematica, 1679

milestones.note: Number-theory content of the volume not checked.

milestones.label: Euler's first proof of Fermat's little theorem
milestones.work: Euler, Theorematum quorundam ad numeros primos spectantium demonstratio, Commentarii Petropolitanae 8 (1741; written 1736)
milestones.description: Euler gave the first proof of the little theorem, among his work that established Fermat's statements as theorems.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E54: written 1736, published 1741, first proof of the little theorem.
Crossref lists a 2020 Spectrum record of E54.

milestones.note: Volume 8 is dated 1736 on its cover but was printed 1741.

notes: Wikipedia pages for Fermat's little theorem, sums of two squares and Fermat's life were rate-limited. The four-square statement and Pell challenge dates were not verified; no naming or institution milestone found. MacTutor Euler confirms his work on Fermat's conjectures (e.g. 2^32+1 divisible by 641 by 1732).

milestones.label: Brouillon project d'une atteinte aux evenemens des rencontres du cone avec un plan
milestones.description: Desargues introduced pencils, ranges, involution and points at infinity, treating conics through properties invariant under projection.

evidence.claim: Describes the 1639 text: involutions, infinite points, unified theory of conics.
Cites the 1639 'Rough draft for an essay on plane sections of a cone'.
Modern edition record (Oeuvres de Desargues, 2011).

milestones.note: Few copies printed; only one survives, found 1951 (MacTutor). Earlier 1636 perspective tract exists.

milestones.label: Desargues' perspective theorem first published
milestones.description: The theorem on triangles in perspective appeared in print through Bosse's perspective book.

evidence.claim: Perspective theorem first published in 1648 in a work by Bosse.
Records of Bosse's Desargues-based books.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: La maniere universelle de Mr Desargues, 1643

milestones.note: Exact book/year taken from MacTutor; the archive record shown is the 1643 Bosse book.

milestones.label: Poncelet's Traite des proprietes projectives
milestones.work: Poncelet, Traite des proprietes projectives des figures, Paris, 1822
milestones.description: First systematic textbook-style development of projective geometry as a subject.

evidence.claim: Record shows 1865 reprint of the Traite.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Traite des proprietes projectives, 1865 reprint

milestones.note: 1822 first-edition year is background knowledge; only a 1865 reprint found.

milestones.label: Poudra edition of Desargues' works
milestones.description: The collected works were republished, bringing Desargues back after La Hire's copy resurfaced.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1864 Poudra edition.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Oeuvres de Desargues, 1864

evidence.claim: Work rediscovered and republished 1864.

notes: Pascal's Essay pour les coniques (1640) is plausible but not verified. 'Perspective (art)' in the harvest 'from' field is supported by the Wikipedia biography. Naming of 'projective geometry' not dated; consolidation by Poncelet low confidence.

canonicalName: Saint-Vincent and Sarasa: hyperbolic area and the logarithm

milestones.label: Napier's logarithms
milestones.description: Logarithms as a numerical tool existed before the geometric link.

evidence.claim: Crossref lists the 1614 Descriptio.
evidence.source: Crossref record: Smithsonian Libraries record, issued 1614

milestones.label: Saint-Vincent, Opus geometricum quadraturae circuli et sectionum coni
milestones.work: Saint-Vincent, Opus geometricum quadraturae circuli et sectionum coni, Antwerp, 1647
milestones.description: The book shows equal hyperbola areas for equal ratios of abscissae, the essential geometric logarithm property.

evidence.claim: Record of the 1647 Opus geometricum.
evidence.source: Internet Archive record: Opus geometricum quadraturae circuli, 1647

evidence.claim: The area under xy=k over [a,b] equals that over [c,d] if a/b=c/d.

milestones.note: He does not state the logarithm link (MacTutor).

milestones.label: Sarasa links hyperbola areas to logarithms
milestones.work: Sarasa, Solutio problematis a R. P. Marino Mersenno proposito, Antwerp, 1649
milestones.description: Saint-Vincent's pupil identified the hyperbola area with logarithms.

evidence.claim: Open Library lists Sarasa's Solutio problematis (1649).
Connection made by his pupil Sarasa.

milestones.note: That the 1649 work is where the connection appears is background knowledge; MacTutor Sarasa page was missing.

milestones.label: Mercator's Logarithmotechnia
milestones.description: The hyperbola-area logarithm received a power-series expansion.

evidence.claim: Record of Logarithmotechnia 1668.

milestones.note: Contents (series) not read; MacTutor Mercator slug failed. Whether 'natural logarithm' was named here is unchecked.

notes: The harvest claim that Leibniz tied log to the integral of dy/y was not verified and no milestone is made for it. Wikipedia pages for Saint-Vincent, Sarasa and Natural logarithm were rate-limited; MacTutor has no usable Sarasa page. Naming of 'natural/hyperbolic logarithm' is open.
